services provided by independent practice hygienists. It might be simpler for the committee to
amend this section of the law rather than create a whole new section of law just for dental
hygienists and in the process, create payment parity for all.
Thank you for your consideration and I will be happy to answer any questions you might have.

Re: Testimony Regarding LD 1361
Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson and members of the Committee, I am Brian Duffy, Vice President and General Counsel at Delta Dental Plan of Maine d/b/a Northeast Delta Dental ("Delta Dental"). As Maine's largest dental benefits administrator, Delta Dental administers dental benefits for over 350,000 Mainers and contracts with a network of over 650 dentists, 72 independent practice dental hygienists (IPDHs), and 12 denturists.
Delta Dental neither supports nor opposes LD 1361 but respectfully submits this testimony directing the Committee's attention to two significant problems with the bill. Due to these issues, the proposed bill would be unworkable and would grant preferential treatment to registered dental hygienists (RDHs).
First, proposed 24-A MRSA �2765-B(3)(A) and 24-A MRSA �2847-X(3)(A) both require insurers to "facilitate the ability of the dental hygienist to directly bill the insurer for services that are within the lawful scope of practice of a dental hygienist." These provisions would make dental hygienists unique among licensed dental providers. Dental insurers are not required to accept direct billing from all dentists, denturists, or IPDHs. Such direct billing is reserved for providers who are in-network with insurers. Non-participating providers typically do not bill insurers directly. This is the reason that Maine has an assignment of benefits law at 24-A M.R.S. �2827-A. Proposed 24-A MRSA �2765-B(3)(A) and 24-A MRSA �2847-X(3)(A) undermine the benefits of network participation, render assignment of benefits rules unnecessary, and privilege RDHs over other licensed dental providers.
Second, the language at proposed 24-A MRSA �2765-B(3)(B) and 24-A MRSA �2847-X(3)(B) requiring that hygienists be reimbursed at a rate no lower than the "rate for providing the same services as a dentist" is unworkable. Dental insurers may reimburse dentists at different rates depending upon whether they participate in the insurer's network and then upon which network the dentist participates in. For example, Delta Dental maintains three separate dentist networks in the state of Maine, each of which is reimbursed at a different rate. Non-participating dentists are reimbursed at still a different rate. The proposed payment parity provisions do not clarify how to assess parity when dentists may be paid at different rates. Moreover, existing law requiring insurers to pay for covered services rendered by IPDHs, 24-A MRSA �2847-Q, does not require payment parity with dentists (though Northeast Delta Dental does reimburse IPDHs at the same rate it reimburses dentists in our general practitioner PPO network). As with the first set

of provisions discussed above, proposed 24-A MRSA �2765-B(3)(B) and 24-A MRSA �2847-X(3)(B) privilege RDHs over other licensed professionals. More significantly, the payment parity provisions cannot be implemented because payment rates vary.
These issues could be addressed by copying the example of 24-A MRSA �2847-Q. This statute was enacted to require that insurers cover services rendered by IPDHs if such services would be covered when rendered by dentists. The goal of LD 1361 is the same. Amending LD 1361 to consist of a revised � 2847-X that matches � 2847-Q but replaces " independent practice dental hygienist" with "dental hygienist" would alleviate the concerns mentioned above and align the treatment of IPDHs and RDHs in statute.
Sincerely,

Testimony of Courtney Vannah, IPDH, MS, MPH Coordinator, IPDH Networking Group
LD 1361: An Act to Require Insurance Coverage for Covered Dental Services Provided by Licensed Dental Hygienists and to Authorize Licensed Dental Hygienists to Bill Commercial
Dental Insurance Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services
Public Hearing: April 24, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services. My name is Courtney Vannah, and I live in Waldoboro. I am here today on behalf of the Independent Practice Dental Hygiene (IPDH) Networking Group and I urge you to support LD 1361.
This bill aligns Maine's insurance code with the Maine Dental Practice Act statutes pertaining to the practice of dental hygiene. The last time Maine's insurance code was amended regarding reimbursement of dental hygienists to add language about reimbursement of IPDHs, the Practice Act required supervision of Registered Dental Hygienists (RDHs) by a dentist. Therefore, Maine's insurance code did not include language requiring insurers to recognize the RDH as a reimbursable provider because services rendered by an RDH were billed under a dentist's license. However, since that time, the Practice Act has been revised to remove supervision requirements for RDH services -- a significant step towards access to preventive and early intervention care for Maine residents. However, one issue stands in the way of direct access to RDH services: the inability to be reimbursed by commercial insurers. A vote in favor of this bill would remove that barrier.
The IPDH Networking Group includes a number of practicing IPDHs in Maine who gather periodically to discuss issues affecting their practice. One such issue voiced by this group is that some payors reimburse them a lower rate than the exact same service provided by a dental hygienist that is billed under the license of a dentist. This inequity puts Maine's IPDHs at an unfair disadvantage when Maine relies on them for the increase in access to preventive and early intervention care they bring to thousands of patients, particularly children, who would otherwise not have access. A vote in favor of this bill would make it illegal for any dental hygienist to be reimbursed unfairly for equivalent services.
A vote in favor of this bill is a vote in favor of equity in care, fairness in reimbursement practices, and support for Maine's dental hygienist. We ask you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1361 to support access to oral healthcare.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I welcome any questions.

Testimony in Support of LD 1361 - "An Act to Require Insurance Coverage for Covered Dental Services Provided by Licensed Dental Hygienists and to Authorize Licensed Dental Hygienists to Bill Commercial Insurance"
Dear Senator Bailey, Representative Perry, and distinguished members of the Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services Committee,
My name is Kala Myers-French, and I am a licensed Independent Practice Dental Hygienist (IPDH) in Camden, Maine. I also serve as the founder of Balanced Dental Hygiene Suite, an integrative dental hygiene practice, and as Executive Director of Maine Oral Health & Wellness, a nonprofit mobile dental program serving underserved children and working families across the state.
I'm writing today in strong support of LD 1361, which is vital not just for dental hygienists, but for the overall health and accessibility of care for Maine residents.
As a provider working in both the private and nonprofit sectors, I face unnecessary barriers every day because I am not allowed to bill all commercial insurance directly. My practice sees patients who cannot otherwise afford care including but not limited our must vulnerable populations the children and elderly--but when I cannot be reimbursed for covered services simply because I'm not billing under a dentist, it restricts my ability to sustainably serve my community. This policy punishes providers who are working on the frontlines of access and prevention.
LD 1361 is not about expanding scope of practice. It is about recognizing the credentials and contributions of licensed dental hygienists who are already legally permitted to provide these services. We are trained, licensed professionals providing preventive and therapeutic care that keeps patients out of the emergency room and reduces overall healthcare costs. We should be reimbursed at the same level as a dentist for providing the services within our scope of practice and I urge you to also advocate for equity in the fee schedules utilized for hygienists as the care provided does not change whether we are in the office run by a dentist or practicing on our own. I could actually argue that we are able to provide a more profound preventive and therapeutic treatment as an IPDH because that is our specialty and focus.
This bill is especially important for hygienists like myself who serve medically underserved areas and operate independently or through nonprofit outreach. Right now, the inability to bill all commercial insurance directly, especially medicare advantage plans, which forces us to turn away patients with insurance, spend hours dealing with billing, or worse, find complicated workarounds that undermine and reduce both patient care and provider sustainability. In my nonprofit mobile program, we could serve hundreds more patients--many of them children--if we were able to bill all commercial insurers directly and equitably.
LD 1361 simply levels the playing field. It ensures that when a dental hygienist provides a covered service that we are licensed to provide, the reimbursement is fair and not dependent on whether a dentist is associated with the claim. That's integrity. That's equity. And that's how we build a sustainable healthcare model in Maine focused on prevention of disease not just restoration of it.
I urge you to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 1361. Your support will directly improve access to dental care across our state and recognize the value of the hygienists doing this critical work.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Kala Myers-French, IPDH Balanced Dental Hygiene Suite & Maine Oral Health & Wellness Camden, Maine

Testimony of Kalie Hess, Associate Director Children's Oral Health Network of Maine
LD 1361: An Act to Require Insurance Coverage for Covered Dental Services Provided by Licensed Dental Hygienists and to Authorize Licensed Dental Hygienists to Bill Commercial Dental Insurance Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services Public Hearing: April 24, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services. My name is Kalie Hess, and I am here today on behalf of the Children's Oral Health Network of Maine (COHN) to ask for your support on LD 1361.
COHN is a network of trusted organizations and individuals united by a shared vision: a Maine where all children can grow up free from preventable dental disease. Despite limited resources, our partners work creatively and persistently to bring quality oral health care to children across the state amid a growing oral health crisis. Our legislative efforts largely fall in the Health and Human Services Committee and we have worked in partnership with them over several legislative sessions to advance bipartisan solutions to address Maine's oral health crisis. I am grateful for the opportunity today to speak with your committee on the importance of this bill as part of the solution to this crisis.
Maine is facing an acute workforce shortage in the oral health field. One key strategy to address this challenge is enabling dental hygienists to work at the top of their license. By fully utilizing their skills and training, we can expand access to high-quality care across the state. That's why we strongly support efforts to ensure hygienists are equitably recognized, supported, and empowered in their roles. Hygienists are essential partners in addressing our state's pediatric oral health crisis. We rely on them to lead innovative, community-based initiatives that reach children where they are--in schools, early childhood programs, and other community settings--often outside the traditional dental office model of care delivery.
This bill helps address an outdated and overly narrow approach to delivering dental care. With only 20% of children with MaineCare and 56% with commercial dental insurance having a dental home, we must expand care beyond the walls of traditional dental offices to reach more children (and adults).1 This requires supporting provider models that value the training, expertise, and scope of hygienists.

Dear Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson, and Members of the Committee:
The Bureau of Insurance is neither for nor against L.D. 1361. The purpose of this letter is to provide you with background information and to point out two provisions that should be addressed if the Committee decides to support this bill.
The bill requires insurers to provide coverage for services provided by dental hygienists if the services are covered under the policy and within the lawful scope of practice of a dental hygienist. The insurer must reimburse the dental hygienist for services in the same manner and at the same rate it reimburses a dentist, and the insurer must facilitate the ability of the dental hygienist to directly bill the insurer. The requirements apply to individual and group plans offered by insurers and Title 24 nonprofits (including Delta Dental) beginning January 1, 2026.
However, the bill does not apply to HMOs. This may be a drafting error that the Committee may wish to address.
This bill goes well beyond the usual requirements of provider mandates by requiring carriers to provide equal rates of reimbursement. The other significant change from existing law is that the bill would allow all dental hygienists to bill insurers directly, even when the hygienists are employed by a dental practice and working under the direct supervision of a dentist. As worded, the bill appears to apply to both in- and out-of-network providers. It also implies that hygienists employed by network dentists would need to be credentialed separately from the supervising dentist, a meaningful departure from current requirements.

My name is Traci Dempsey and I am a registered dental hygienist from Bath, Maine. I am also the President of the Maine Dental Hygienists' Association. I am testifying in support of LD1361. I
The intent of this bill is to increase access to care and this is how this bill would impact this issue. Currently we have dental hygienists in schools seeing children. These dental hygienists are able to bill Mainecare at this time but they are unable to bill traditional dental insurance. Many times a child will be
signed up for dental care at school and parents indicate that this child has Mainecare. The dental
hygienist verifies the child has Mainecare and proceeds with treatment. When the provider bills
Mainecare the claim is rejected because the child also has traditional insurance that was not disclosed prior to treatment. Traditional dental insurance must be billed as the primary insurance and Mainecare
becomes secondary insurance. Now the dental hygienist is unable to be paid for the services they have
rendered because they are not able to bill the dental insurance first and must write off the care they
provided to that child. This presents a big challenge to dental hygienists providing care in school
settings.
Data shows 20% of children with Mainecare have no dental home and 56% of children with traditional dental insurance do not have a dental home. This tells me we are missing an opportunity to meet these children where they are nine months out of the year. Many parents have transportation issues or are
unable to get into a traditional dental practice to have their child seen. This change could have a huge impact on Maine's schoolchildren.
There has been previous legislation passed to allow independent dental hygienists to bill traditional
dental insurance. It is my understanding that we will hear testimony in support of adopting that
language but adapted for dental hygienists as a whole. We would also be in support of that language
change. For reference that language is found at 24-A MRSA �2847-Q. This would mean replacing the
